analysis.one_liner: Lets corporations and unions fund election ads without disclosing spending.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo key parts of the 2002 campaign finance law (the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act, often called McCain-Feingold). It would wipe out three rules about "electioneering communications" — TV and radio ads that mention a federal candidate close to an election. First, it would end the requirement that whoever pays for those ads report the spending to the Federal Election Commission, so the public would no longer learn who was behind the ads. Second, it would let corporations and labor unions pay for those ads directly out of their own treasuries, which the 2002 law had banned. Third, it would stop treating ads a candidate's campaign coordinates with an outside group as a campaign contribution subject to donation limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and labor unions would gain the ability to pay for broadcast ads supporting or attacking federal candidates right before elections, without filing public reports about it. Corporate treasuries, which vastly outsize union funds, would be the biggest winners, since they could sway elections with money that never had to be traced to them.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the rule that anyone paying for electioneering communications must file a spending report with the FEC, ending public disclosure of who funded the ads [S2][S3].
Repeals the ban on corporations and labor organizations making electioneering communications, allowing them to fund candidate-focused broadcast ads directly [S2][S3].
Removes the provision treating coordinated communications as contributions, so ads coordinated with a campaign would no longer count against donation limits [S2][S3].
The bill's stated rationale, reflected in its title, is that these rules burden political speech protected by the First Amendment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Voters would bear the cost of losing information: ads flooding the airwaves before elections could be paid for by corporations or unions with no public record of who was behind them. Candidates and parties would also face uncoordinated spending that could not be tracked or limited through coordination rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters, who lose disclosure of ad funders

drawbacks.text: Ending disclosure means voters could no longer see who paid for ads that urge them to support or oppose a candidate, removing information central to judging political messages [S2][S3].
Allowing corporate treasury spending on election ads would shift influence toward wealthy corporations, since corporate funds dwarf union funds available for the same purpose [S2].
Removing the treatment of coordinated communications as contributions would open a path around contribution limits for well-funded outside groups [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is a freer hand for corporations and unions to speak in elections, which its sponsor framed as a First Amendment matter. The cost falls on voters, who would lose the disclosure records that show who is trying to influence their votes, and on campaign finance limits, which coordinated spending could evade. The gains flow overwhelmingly to organizations with large treasuries — chiefly corporations — rather than to ordinary voters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the new Congress, referred to the House Administration Committee, attracted no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Roscoe Bartlett introduced the bill on January 4, 2005, the opening day of the 109th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, which held jurisdiction over election law, the same day [S5].
No cosponsor signed on, no further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much, since the bill never advanced. Voters kept the disclosure and funding rules in place under the 2002 law, so corporate and union treasuries did not obtain the unrestricted, unreported election spending the bill would have allowed.

for.name: Rep. Roscoe Bartlett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over election and campaign finance law
against.what_they_did: Took no action after receiving the referral — no markup, hearing, or vote — letting the bill expire

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors of either party, so its support never took a partisan shape [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have let corporate treasuries fund candidate-focused broadcast ads without any public disclosure of the spending. That gain comes directly at the public's expense, since voters would no longer know who paid for the ads trying to influence them [S2][S3].
Loosening the rules would likely increase paid political advertising, a revenue source for TV and radio stations. More ads also mean more persuasion aimed at viewers, which cuts both ways [S2].

The bill would have lifted the same ban on unions that it lifted on corporations, letting union funds pay for election ads. Union political spending generally backs candidates and causes aligned with their members' interests [S2].
